title: Will they remember you?
principle: People buy the names that come to mind first.

screens.text: Let me tell you about a small dog. In the early 2000s, a phone company called Hutch made ads showing a pug following a boy everywhere. The line was: "Wherever you go, our network follows." People loved the pug, and more people in India began buying pugs.

screens.prompt: In 2007, Vodafone bought Hutch and changed its name to Vodafone. What do you think it did with the pug?

options.label: Stopped using it and tried something new
Kept using it with the new name
Replaced it with a famous film star

screens.why: Vodafone kept the pug. In the new ad, the pug left a pink dog house, Hutch's colour, and walked into a red one, Vodafone's colour. The name changed, but people still saw the dog they remembered.

screens.title: Mental availability
screens.text: Byron Sharp, a marketing professor, calls this mental availability. It means how easily people remember your name when they want to buy. People choose from names they remember. Even a better shop may lose buyers if nobody thinks of it.

screens.title: Things that remind them
screens.text: So what makes people remember your name? Things they link to you, like a colour, a sound or a character like the pug. These are called distinctive brand assets. Even a funny line people repeat can help them remember you.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: Phone networks are huge, but people can forget small bakeries too. It's the first week of December. You pack every cake in a pink box. A mother who loved your cake in March just bought her son's birthday cake from a chain shop. She said, "I forgot your name."

screens.prompt: True or false: if your cake really is the best, families will remember you.

options.label: True: a great cake sells itself
False: they must also remember your name

screens.why: False. The mother loved your cake, but months later, your name didn't come to mind. When it's time to buy, people pick what they remember.

wrong.a: Many bakers think so. But the mother loved your cake and still bought from another shop. Months later, she couldn't remember your name. A great cake alone isn't enough.

screens.prompt: Which will help families remember your bakery months later?

options.label: A new box design every month
The same pink box on every cake

screens.why: Yes. When families see the same pink box again and again, they start linking it to your bakery. That's how the pug became linked to Hutch.

wrong.a: New designs may look nice, but families won't know which one is yours. Use the same pink box every time, so people start linking it to you.
wrong.b: A discount may bring an order, but people may remember only the offer. When they see your pink box again and again, they start linking it to you.

screens.prompt: Which WhatsApp status line will families repeat to their friends?

options.label: "Fresh cakes ready. Order now on WhatsApp."
"Best quality cakes at the best price."

screens.why: Exactly. It's short, funny and easy to remember. You post it with your name and number every time. So when people share the line, they can share your name too.

wrong.b: It's clear, but many bakers say the same thing. People have seen it many times, so they may not repeat it. A short, funny line is easier to share.
wrong.c: Many shops say "best quality, best price", so people may not notice it. A short, funny line is easier to remember and share.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six things a baker might do. For each one, tell me: will it help families remember you?

items.text: The same pink box on every cake
A new logo every few months
Your name and number on a sticker on every box
A different name on WhatsApp and Instagram
The same funny line at the end of every post
Posting only when you have an offer

screens.why: When families see the same things often, they start remembering your bakery. But if you keep changing your name and logo, they may forget you. Posting only offers doesn't help them remember your shop.

screens.setup: It's the first week of December. Christmas and New Year parties are coming. You have ₹10,000 to spend so families remember you. Each cake leaves you ₹450. About 500 families have bought from you this year.
screens.question: How do you spend it?

options.label: Spend ₹10,000 on one big newspaper ad
options.outcome: Many people see your ad once, but most forget it by the next day. You get 8 new orders in December and earn ₹3,600. That's ₹6,400 less than what you spent on the ad.
options.why: People soon forget an ad they see only once. They need to see your name often, especially when they want to buy.
options.better: Give past buyers something with your name and number that they'll see every day.

options.label: Spend ₹10,000 on a new name and logo
options.outcome: Your new name, logo and boxes cost ₹10,000. They look nice. But families who knew "the pink box baker" can no longer find you. December orders fall by 10. You lose ₹4,500, besides the ₹10,000 you spent.
options.why: You changed the things families remembered about you. Even Vodafone kept the pug when it changed its name.
options.better: Give past buyers something with your name and number that they'll see every day.

options.label: Give 500 past buyers pink magnets with your number
options.outcome: Each magnet costs ₹20. You give one with every order and deliver the rest to past buyers. When families plan a party, they see your number on the fridge. You get 25 extra orders in December and earn ₹11,250, more than you spent. The magnets stay useful.
options.why: Your colour and number stay on the fridge, where families see them every day. So when they want to buy a cake, they may remember you first.

screens.title: The honest line
screens.text: The line again: use on others only what you'd accept being used on you. Helping people remember your shop is fair. But copying a famous shop's colours to make buyers think your cakes are theirs is cheating. You wouldn't like someone doing that to you.
People buy the names that come to ___ first, so make yours easy to ___.
screens.why: Exactly. Vodafone kept the pug because people remembered it. Your pink box, funny line and fridge magnet help families remember your bakery too.

summary: Mental availability: when people want to buy, they choose from names they remember.
Distinctive brand assets: use the same colour, look and funny line often.
Even a great product may not sell if people forget your name. Never copy another brand's look.

cards.front: Your ghee is better than a famous brand, but buyers don't know its name. Which will they buy?
cards.back: People choose from the names they remember when they want to buy.

cards.front: What helps buyers remember your shop?
options: A new logo every few months
The same colour and look every time
cards.back: Distinctive brand assets: keep one look, and show it often.

cards.front: A big company buys yours and changes the name. What should it keep?
options: Things buyers remember, like a mascot
cards.back: Vodafone kept Hutch's pug. Keep the thing people link to you.
